passages.happening:
The book begins with a bare list of names: ‘Adam, Seth, Enosh’ (verse 1), down to Noah and his three sons (verses 1-4). Then come the peoples that came from Noah's sons: Japheth (verses 5-7), Ham (verses 8-16) and Shem (verses 17-23). The line of Shem runs straight down to ‘Abram (that is, Abraham)’ (verse 27).

Only two small notes break into the names. Nimrod ‘began to be a mighty one on the earth’ (verse 10), and Peleg was so named ‘because in his days the earth was divided’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The Chronicler begins Israel's story not with Abraham, Moses or David, but with Adam. In Hebrew adam is also the ordinary word for a human being. The first word of the book says that Israel's history belongs inside the history of humanity, and that its God is the God of every nation.

The names come from Genesis 5, 10 and 11, heavily shortened. No stories are told, because the readers already knew them. Many of the names in verses 5 to 23 are peoples and places as much as persons: Javan is the Greeks, Mizraim is Egypt, Cush lies south of Egypt, Asshur is Assyria, Aram is Syria. A father in a genealogy might be a founder of a town or a people.

For readers after the exile a genealogy was not a hobby. It was a claim about who belonged, who could inherit and who could serve as priest. Beginning with Adam told a small people under a foreign empire that their identity rested on a longer line than any empire's.

What the division in Peleg's days means is not said. Many connect it with the scattering of languages at Babel; others think of land divided by channels.
passages.later: Luke traces Jesus' family back past Abraham and David to ‘the son of Adam, the son of God’ (Luke 3:38).
passages.hard:
Why would a book of history begin with nine chapters of names, and do the names always agree with Genesis?

For the first readers the genealogies were the most urgent part of the book. A people back from exile, with no king and little land, needed to know that they were still Israel and still joined to God's purposes from the beginning. The lists are an argument for identity, not filler.

The names mostly follow Genesis closely, with small differences in spelling. Rodanites in verse 7 corresponds to Dodanim in Genesis 10:4, since the Hebrew letters d and r look very alike, and the Greek translation of Genesis has Rhodians there, which agrees with the r. Other small variations come from copying or from different ways of spelling foreign names. Readers who hold to the Bible's full reliability treat them as questions of how the text was handed down, and scholars of every view see the Chronicler following Genesis carefully rather than inventing.
passages.asks: The book opens with the whole human family before it narrows to Israel. Ask what it means that your story, and the church's, sits inside the story of every people. And ask who you have treated as outside God's interest.

passages.t: Abraham's sons, Esau, and the kings of Edom
passages.happening:
‘The sons of Abraham were Isaac and Ishmael’ (verse 28). The chapter lists Ishmael's twelve sons and the sons Keturah bore to Abraham (verses 29-33). Then ‘Abraham was the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel’ (verse 34).

Esau's family comes next, with the older people of Seir (verses 35-42). The chapter ends with ‘the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites’ (verse 43), and with Edom's chiefs (verses 51-54).
passages.hearers:
The chapter follows a pattern Genesis also uses. The lines that do not carry the promise are dealt with first and then set aside: Ishmael and Keturah's sons before Isaac, and Esau before Israel. Being listed first did not mean being rejected. It meant the story was about to narrow.

Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea, was by the Chronicler's time a neighbor with a long and bitter history with Judah, and Edomites had moved into southern Judah after Jerusalem fell. Yet Esau is here as Israel's brother. The note that Edom had kings before Israel did is a reminder that monarchy came late to Israel.

The chapter moves from the widest circle, all humanity, to the nations, to Abraham's family, to Isaac's sons, and it ends in Edom with kings and chiefs, which looks ahead to the royal story to come.
passages.later: God told Abraham, ‘all the families of the earth will be blessed through you’ (Genesis 12:3), and Paul read that promise as the gospel announced ahead of time to the nations (Galatians 3:8).
passages.asks: Esau and Ishmael are named and kept in the record, though the story moves on without them. Ask how you treat people whose part in your story is over. And ask what it means that God's promise narrowed to one family for the sake of all families.
